Supported condition keys: dayMin, dayMax, spiritDryMin, spiritDryMax, contactsTodayMin, contactsTodayMax, paydayToday (bool), setbackToday (bool), langLevelUpToday (bool), noActionsToday (bool), hadDeepVisitToday_<npcId> (bool).

reflections.text: Tokyo settles. Somewhere a vending machine hums in an empty alley.
A train passes far below. The window glass cools against your forehead.
You think of one face from today. Just one. You pray for them by name.
The kanji on the sign across the street is one you didn't know last month.
Someone you don't know is laughing two floors up. The wall carries it down.
You wonder, briefly, what your supporters back home are doing right now.
The kettle clicks off. Steam in the small kitchen. Nothing else.
A neon sign blinks. Tokyo doesn't sleep — but tonight, you do.
You write one line in your journal. You close it before you read it back.
Tomorrow, you tell yourself, will be its own day.
Some days don't open. You don't know why. You set the day down anyway, gently, and trust it to keep without you.
You sit with the quiet you've been avoiding. There's nothing here to fight. Maybe that's the point.
The wire came in around three. Names you don't know in a town you remember. People keeping you here, paycheck by paycheck.
Money came in. Faces came by. Some days the resources align for no reason you can name.
You realize tonight that you understood the train announcement without translating it first. Small thing. Doesn't feel small.
Your face hurts from smiling at strangers. Good day. Tomorrow your throat will remember it.
Two faces today. You replay both conversations in your head. One went well. The other you wish you had said differently.
No new faces today. The city is loud and you walked through most of it unheard. Tomorrow.
Kenji said more than usual tonight. You'll be careful with what you do with that.
Yuki's questions don't have easy answers. You think about hers more than you think about your own.
You think of Hiro's bench. Of the pigeons. Of how some grief doesn't need anyone to fix it — just sit with it.
You did almost nothing today. That happens. Even Jesus slept.
The well feels dry tonight. You pray anyway — not because it lifts the dryness, but because it's what missionaries do when nothing else makes sense.
A month in. The city is starting to feel less like a foreign country and more like a place you walk through.
You've been here long enough that the convenience store clerk near your building greets you by name. Small thing. Means something.
